name: Tazarotenic acid

lead: Tazarotenic acid is what the body makes from tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid used for acne, psoriasis and photodamage. The payoff people want is fewer wrinkles, even tone and smoother texture; some forum users describe tazarotene as stronger than tretinoin.

Skin and blood esterases convert tazarotene to tazarotenic acid, which binds retinoic acid receptors, selectively RAR-beta and RAR-gamma, altering skin-cell growth and differentiation. A 12-month trial of tazarotene cream showed improvement in wrinkles and pigmentation versus vehicle. No studies have tested the acid alone.

paras: People encounter it only through tazarotene, a prescription cream or gel. Photoaging changes in trials built over months of regular use.
Irritation is the most common effect of the parent drug. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and is prescription-only in the US.

angle.text: Tazarotenic acid is the active form that prescription tazarotene converts into on skin, where it binds retinoic acid receptors to boost renewal and smooth wrinkles and pigmentation. A 12-month trial covers the parent drug; the acid alone is not sold.

lead: Tazarotenic acid is the active form of tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid used for acne, plaque psoriasis and signs of photoaging such as fine lines, wrinkles, uneven pigmentation and sun spots. Tazarotene is a prodrug: after it is applied, esterase enzymes in the skin and blood remove its ethyl ester group, producing the free acid that binds retinoic acid receptors [1][2]. People get tazarotenic acid only through tazarotene, sold under brand names such as Tazorac, Arazlo and Fabior and as generics.

The appearance chain is direct. Tazarotene is converted to tazarotenic acid, which acts on receptors that govern how skin cells grow and differentiate, and in a 12-month trial in people with facial photodamage the cream improved fine wrinkling, mottled pigmentation and sun spots compared with vehicle [3][1]. Acne improvement is also documented [4].

Tazarotenic acid binds retinoic acid receptors (RARs) but not retinoid X receptors, and in laboratory assays it is selective for the RAR-beta and RAR-gamma subtypes [5][1]. In online skincare discussion, tazarotene is described by some users as a stronger alternative to tretinoin for texture and anti-aging. No published study has tested tazarotenic acid as a stand-alone cosmetic ingredient; the human evidence concerns the parent drug.

paras: Tazarotene is approved for acne and plaque psoriasis and can reduce photoaging signs including fine lines, wrinkles, hyperpigmentation and lentigines; Wikipedia notes that daily sunscreen use improves results. In acne it is often combined with benzoyl peroxide or an oral antibiotic, and in psoriasis it is paired with a corticosteroid, which can also reduce irritation.

Tazarotene was first approved as a gel in 1997, followed by 0.05% and 0.1% creams in 2000, a 0.1% foam in 2012 and a 0.045% lotion in 2019, and a fixed-dose combination with halobetasol (Duobrii) is approved for psoriasis.

Retinoids are grouped by generation. Tretinoin and isotretinoin are first-generation natural retinoic acids; adapalene, bexarotene and tazarotene are third-generation synthetic benzoic acid derivatives; and trifarotene, approved in the US in 2019, is a fourth-generation compound selective for RAR-gamma [6]. Tazarotene's narrower receptor targeting differs from the broader RAR and RXR binding of the natural acids [6]. Retinoic acid signalling is central to regulating skin cell growth and differentiation [6].

Tazarotene belongs to the acetylenic retinoids, a class whose structure resists isomerization. Its free acid, tazarotenic acid, binds RARs and not RXRs, and gene-activation assays indicate selectivity for the RAR-beta and RAR-gamma subtypes [5][1]. Through these receptors it is described as slowing keratinocyte proliferation and promoting differentiation, and reviews also discuss comedolytic and anti-inflammatory properties of topical retinoids [7].

After topical application, only a few percent of the dose reaches the stratum corneum and viable epidermis, and a review of the drug's pharmacokinetics describes limited absorption into the bloodstream, with less than about 6% of the applied dose absorbed [8][9]. Tazarotene is converted by esterases in human blood and liver to tazarotenic acid [2]. Tazarotenic acid is then further metabolized, with cytochrome P450 2C8 and flavin-containing monooxygenases implicated in humans [10]. Over 99% is bound to plasma proteins and it is eliminated in urine and feces.
No studies found of tazarotenic acid administered on its own. Human trials have tested its parent drug, tazarotene.

In a 24-week double-blind trial of 563 people with facial photodamage, followed by a 28-week open-label extension, 0.1% tazarotene cream produced significantly more improvement than vehicle in fine wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, lentigines and other signs; improvement had not plateaued by week 52. Twenty of 283 tazarotene-treated participants and 1 of 280 vehicle participants stopped because of adverse events, and plasma tazarotenic acid stayed at or below 0.71 ng/mL [3]. Pooled results of two vehicle-controlled trials examined 0.1% tazarotene cream in facial acne [4]. Registered trials have also looked at tazarotene in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and scalp psoriasis [11][12].

Skin irritation (redness, itching, burning) is the most commonly reported effect of tazarotene and tends to rise with concentration. A review of tazarotene safety concluded that systemic exposure is minimal and found no association with contact sensitization, phototoxicity or carcinogenicity [9]. Tazarotene is nonetheless labelled as contraindicated in pregnancy, a position based on animal studies.

The FDA originally classed tazarotene as Category X, stricter than the Category C given to adapalene and tretinoin, and after lettered categories were dropped in 2015 it was still deemed contraindicated, based on animal teratogenicity data because human pregnancy data are lacking. The American Academy of Dermatology advises against topical retinoids in pregnancy, and a 2026 Nordic cohort study reported no rise in birth defects with topical retinoid use [6].

Users of prescription retinoids discuss tazarotene as a step up in strength from tretinoin or adapalene, and are more likely to talk about the brand-name product than about the metabolite. Its irritation profile, which Wikipedia says increases with concentration, is a frequent topic.

Preclinical work suggests tazarotene may slow melanoma growth through tazarotene-induced genes (TIG1, TIG2, TIG3), by suppressing mTOR signalling and promoting differentiation and immune-cell recruitment; this is early-stage laboratory research. Researchers have developed nanoparticle formulations of tazarotene intended to deliver it to hair follicles in inflammatory skin disease [13].
